Problem: The 50%-task-completion time horizon metric has been validated primarily for software engineering tasks, leaving open whether this compelling capability measure generalizes to other knowledge-work domains with different error structures, tool requirements, and verification challenges. Understanding cross-domain time horizons is critical for anticipating where AI automation will next reach human-level capability.

Proposed Method: We extend the time horizon framework to three non-software professional domains: (1) scientific data analysis (biology/chemistry lab pipelines), (2) legal document work (contract review, case research, memo drafting), and (3) financial analysis (modeling, due diligence, report generation). For each domain, we recruit 20+ professionals, instrument task completion times using structured protocols, and build domain-specific benchmark suites (50-200 tasks spanning 5-minute to 8-hour human completion times). We evaluate frontier models (GPT-5, Claude 4, Gemini 2.x) on these benchmarks to compute domain-specific time horizons, then analyze whether the ~7-month doubling rate observed in software holds, accelerates, or lags across domains.

Experiments: (1) Human timing studies per domain, (2) AI evaluation with standardized scaffolding, (3) regression analysis of domain-specific scaling curves, (4) qualitative analysis of failure modes distinguishing domains, (5) cross-domain correlation analysis to identify whether software time horizons predict non-software horizons, enabling earlier capability forecasting.

title: Decomposing the Time Horizon Metric: Disentangling Reliability, Reasoning, and Tool Use as Drivers of AI Task Completion Capability
description: Problem: The 50%-task-completion time horizon metric aggregates AI capability into a single scalar, but the anchor paper hypothesizes that gains stem from distinct factors: reliability/error recovery, logical reasoning, and tool use. Experiments: Correlation analysis between benchmark time horizons and field-measured AI leverage; stratified analysis by task type (bug fixing, feature development, refactoring); regression models testing whether time horizon predicts productivity gains better than existing benchmarks (SWE-bench, HumanEval); and qualitative coding of failure modes where benchmark performance does not transfer. We test whether time horizon metrics derived from uninterrupted tasks overestimate real-world autonomous capability, and identify which architectural features (extended context, tool-use memory) most predict resumption robustness.

title: Decomposing the Time Horizon Gap: Diagnosing Where Long-Task AI Performance Breaks Down

title: Task Decomposition Horizons: Measuring Whether AI Can Autonomously Break Down and Delegate Month-Long Software Projects

title: Beyond Time Horizons: Measuring AI Reliability Degradation Curves Across Task Complexity Strata

title: Task Decomposition Depth as a Predictor of AI Time Horizon Generalization Across Domains

Experiments: (1) Cross-domain time horizon comparison showing variance in current capability levels; (2) Historical reconstruction using archived model outputs to estimate per-domain doubling rates since 2021; (3) Feature importance analysis identifying which domain properties most predict faster AI capability growth; (4) Correlation analysis between benchmark saturation speed and time horizon growth across domains.

title: Beyond Completion Rate: Measuring AI Code Quality Degradation Across Extended Software Tasks
description:
Problem: The 50%-task-completion time horizon metric captures whether AI completes tasks but ignores solution quality dimensions critical for real-world deployment—code maintainability, security vulnerabilities, test coverage, and architectural soundness. A model completing a 50-minute task in 10 minutes with brittle, insecure code may be worse than no automation at all. Current benchmarks treat task completion as binary, masking systematic quality-time tradeoffs as task complexity scales.

Proposed Method: We introduce a Quality-Adjusted Time Horizon (QATH) metric that augments completion rate with multi-dimensional quality scoring. For each completed task, we assess: (1) static analysis metrics (cyclomatic complexity, security linting), (2) test coverage of generated solutions, (3) peer review scores from senior engineers blind to AI authorship, and (4) downstream breakage rates when integrated into larger codebases. We examine how quality scores degrade as task duration increases from 5 minutes to 8 hours, controlling for completion rate.

Experiments: We sample 200 tasks spanning 5-minute to 4-hour human completion times from SWE-bench, RE-Bench, and novel enterprise tasks. Five frontier models complete each task. Human experts score outputs using a structured rubric. We fit quality-degradation curves per model and compute QATH as the time horizon where both completion rate and quality jointly reach acceptable thresholds, revealing whether capability scaling preserves or sacrifices solution quality.

title: Beyond Software: Measuring AI Time Horizons Across Diverse Professional Domains
description:
Problem: The 50%-task-completion time horizon metric has been validated primarily for software engineering tasks, leaving unclear whether AI capability growth trends generalize to other professional domains like scientific research, legal analysis, financial modeling, or medical diagnosis. Different domains may exhibit distinct scaling trajectories due to varying requirements for tacit knowledge, physical world interaction, regulatory constraints, or domain-specific reasoning.

Proposed Method: We extend the time horizon framework to five non-software professional domains: (1) biomedical research literature synthesis, (2) legal contract analysis and drafting, (3) financial due diligence, (4) data-driven scientific hypothesis generation, and (5) educational curriculum design. For each domain, we recruit credentialed professionals (n=15 per domain) to complete standardized tasks while being timed, establishing human baselines. We then evaluate frontier models (GPT-5, Claude 4, Gemini 2.x) on identical tasks using domain-appropriate scaffolding and tool access, computing 50% time horizons per domain.

Experiments: We compute per-domain time horizons, compare doubling rates across domains and against the software baseline, analyze failure modes using structured error coding, and build regression models identifying which domain characteristics (formalizability, verifiability, knowledge cutoff sensitivity) predict faster AI capability growth. This produces a cross-domain capability map informing both deployment decisions and AI safety prioritization.

title: Calibrating the Time Horizon Metric Across Cognitive Domains: Beyond Software Engineering
description:
Problem: The 50%-task-completion time horizon metric is validated exclusively on software engineering tasks, leaving unclear whether this human-interpretable capability measure generalizes across diverse cognitive domains like scientific reasoning, legal analysis, mathematical research, or creative writing. Domain-specific task structures, failure modes, and human performance distributions may systematically distort horizon estimates in ways that make cross-domain comparisons misleading.

Proposed Method: We extend the time horizon framework to four non-software domains: (1) scientific hypothesis generation and experimental design, (2) legal document analysis and contract drafting, (3) mathematical proof construction, and (4) structured creative writing. For each domain, we recruit 20+ professionals per domain to time-complete a stratified task battery (5-minute to 8-hour tasks), establishing human baseline distributions. We then evaluate 5 frontier models using the same agentic scaffolding approach, computing domain-specific time horizons. We additionally propose a 'horizon calibration factor'—a correction term accounting for task-type variance in human completion time distributions.

Experiments: Primary analysis compares time horizons across domains for identical models, testing whether software-derived horizon estimates transfer. Secondary analysis examines whether the ~7-month doubling rate holds domain-specifically or reflects a software-biased artifact. We further test whether human rater agreement on task difficulty correlates with horizon measurement reliability, informing future benchmark construction methodology.

title: Beyond Time Horizons: Measuring AI Capability Ceilings Through Task Complexity Taxonomies
description: Problem: The 50%-task-completion time horizon metric captures task duration as a proxy for difficulty, but conflates multiple distinct dimensions of software task complexity (e.g., ambiguous requirements, multi-system coordination, domain-specific knowledge depth, iterative stakeholder feedback). This prevents understanding *why* AI systems fail and which capability dimensions are bottlenecks, limiting actionable guidance for capability improvement. Proposed Method: We decompose software task difficulty along five orthogonal axes—specification ambiguity, dependency graph depth, domain knowledge density, error recovery branching, and external API/human-in-the-loop interactions—and construct a benchmark of 200 tasks spanning a controlled factorial design across these axes. We train a 'difficulty predictor' mapping task features to AI success rates across multiple frontier models (GPT-5, Claude 4, Gemini 2.x), enabling per-axis capability profiling rather than a single scalar metric. We further propose a 'ceiling score': the minimum task complexity along any single axis sufficient to reduce AI success below 20%. Planned Experiments: (1) Validate factorial task set with human timing and success rates; (2) run frontier models on all tasks in agentic settings; (3) perform ablation studies isolating which complexity axes most predict failure; (4) test whether capability ceilings from this benchmark predict real-world GitHub issue resolution rates, validating external generalizability beyond the original paper's open concern.

title: Beyond Time Horizons: Measuring AI Capability Degradation Under Resource Constraints and Interruptions in Long-Horizon Software Tasks
description:
Problem: The 50%-task-completion time horizon metric captures average AI performance on software tasks but treats task execution as uninterrupted and resource-unlimited. Real-world software development involves context window limits, compute budgets, mandatory checkpoints, and mid-task requirement changes. We lack understanding of how AI capability degrades under these realistic constraints, creating a gap between benchmark metrics and deployable autonomy.

Proposed Method: We extend the time-horizon framework by introducing a 'capability degradation profile' — measuring how 50% completion rates change as functions of (1) forced mid-task interruptions requiring state reconstruction, (2) context compression events, (3) dynamic requirement amendments introduced at 25%/50%/75% completion, and (4) hard compute-time budgets. We develop a structured interruption protocol applied to RE-Bench and HCAST tasks, instrumenting frontier models (GPT-5, Claude 4, Gemini 2.x) with controlled perturbation injections.

Experiments: We run 500+ task completions across 4 frontier models with a 4×4 factorial design crossing interruption frequency and requirement volatility. We measure degradation curves relative to uninterrupted baselines, identify which task types are most brittle, and correlate degradation patterns with underlying model architecture choices (context length, reasoning depth). Results yield a more deployment-realistic capability metric complementing the existing time-horizon measure.

title: Beyond Completion Rate: Measuring AI Code Quality Degradation Over Extended Task Horizons
description: Problem: Current time-horizon benchmarks measure task completion rate but ignore solution quality dimensions—security vulnerabilities, technical debt, test coverage, and maintainability—that human developers trade off when working under time pressure. An AI system might 'complete' a month-long software task while producing unmaintainable or insecure code, making raw completion rates misleading for real-world deployment decisions. Proposed Method: We extend the 50%-task-completion time horizon framework by introducing a multi-dimensional Quality-Adjusted Task Completion (QATC) metric. For each completed task, we apply automated static analysis (Semgrep, SonarQube), human expert code review, and execution-based testing to score security, maintainability, test coverage, and correctness independently. We then compute quality-weighted time horizons across task durations (5 minutes to 8 hours). We hypothesize that AI quality degrades faster than completion rate as task horizon increases, revealing a 'quality cliff' at longer horizons. Experiments: We sample 200 tasks from RE-Bench/HCAST and novel tasks, collect completions from Claude 3.7 Sonnet, GPT-4o, and Gemini 2.0, score using our rubric, and compare quality-adjusted vs. raw time horizons. We also recruit 30 human developers to establish quality baselines. This reveals whether AI autonomy gains are illusory when accounting for code quality.

title: Decomposing AI Time Horizon Growth: Isolating Contributions of Reasoning, Tool Use, and Error Recovery via Targeted Ablation Benchmarks
description: Problem: While the 50%-task-completion time horizon metric reveals that frontier AI capabilities have been doubling every ~7 months, the paper attributes this growth vaguely to 'reliability, error recovery, logical reasoning, and tool use' without quantitative decomposition. Understanding which capability dimensions drive time horizon expansion is critical for predicting future progress and identifying bottlenecks. Proposed Method: We construct four specialized benchmark suites that systematically isolate each capability dimension: (1) Reasoning-Pure tasks with pre-verified tool scaffolding so only logical planning varies, (2) Tool-Use-Pure tasks with templated reasoning but diverse API/environment interactions, (3) Error-Recovery tasks where intentional faults are injected mid-execution requiring detection and correction, and (4) Long-Horizon Coordination tasks requiring multi-step planning with minimal errors. We measure time-horizon scores for each suite across 8 frontier models spanning 2022-2025, then fit a causal attribution model to decompose aggregate time horizon growth into per-dimension contributions. Experiments: We evaluate GPT-4o, Claude 3.5/3.7, Gemini 2.0/2.5, and open-weight models (Llama 3.3, DeepSeek-R2) on ~200 tasks per suite, recruit domain experts to establish human baselines, and perform ablation via capability-masking prompts. Outcome: A quantitative decomposition revealing which capability axes most predict time horizon growth, informing targeted research prioritization and safety forecasting.

title: Skill Decomposition of AI Time Horizons: Disentangling Which Capabilities Drive Long-Task Performance
description: Problem: While the 50%-task-completion time horizon metric reveals that frontier AI models can handle ~50-minute tasks, it remains unclear which specific capability bottlenecks limit performance on longer tasks. The paper identifies 'reliability,' 'error recovery,' 'logical reasoning,' and 'tool use' as contributors, but lacks a rigorous causal decomposition that could guide targeted improvements. Proposed Method: We construct a taxonomized benchmark of 500+ software tasks (spanning 5 minutes to 8 hours of human effort) where each task is annotated along four capability axes: error recovery frequency, multi-step planning depth, external tool invocations required, and context window utilization. We then train sparse linear probes on intermediate model activations and action traces to predict task success, attributing performance variance to each axis via Shapley value decomposition. We further conduct ablation experiments using scaffolding interventions (e.g., forcing explicit planning steps, providing error summaries) to causally test each factor's contribution. Experiments: Evaluate Claude 3.7 Sonnet, GPT-5, Gemini 2.0, and DeepSeek-R2 on the benchmark; compare Shapley attributions across model families; test whether targeted scaffolding for the dominant bottleneck disproportionately extends time horizons; measure whether improvements generalize across task domains (web dev, data science, systems programming).

title: Beyond Time Horizons: Measuring AI Capability Degradation Under Real-World Task Interference Conditions
description: Problem: The 50%-task-completion time horizon metric captures average AI capability on isolated tasks, but real-world software development involves constant interruptions, shifting requirements, and multi-task context switching. Current benchmarks don't measure how AI performance degrades when tasks are interleaved, requirements change mid-execution, or the agent must resume after interruption—conditions ubiquitous in professional software work. Proposed Method: We introduce the 'Degraded Horizon' framework, extending the time horizon metric to adversarial real-world conditions. We construct a benchmark (InterruptBench) with three interference modes: (1) mid-task requirement perturbations at varying completion percentages, (2) forced context interruptions requiring task resumption after N unrelated tasks, and (3) conflicting instructions from simulated stakeholders. We measure how the 50% time horizon shrinks under each condition compared to isolated baselines, yielding a 'resilience ratio' metric. We also measure recovery strategies—does the model restart, patch, or abandon? Experiments: We evaluate Claude 3.7 Sonnet, GPT-5, Gemini 2.0, and open-source frontier models (Llama 4, DeepSeek V3) across 200 software tasks spanning the original RE-Bench/HCAST difficulty range. We conduct human timing studies under identical interference conditions to establish calibrated comparison points, enabling honest assessment of whether AI autonomy extrapolations hold in realistic deployment contexts.

title: Beyond Software: Measuring AI Time Horizons Across Heterogeneous Task Domains
description: Problem: The 50%-task-completion time horizon metric was validated primarily on software engineering tasks, leaving open whether this metric generalizes across fundamentally different cognitive domains (scientific research, legal analysis, financial modeling, creative writing, hardware design). Domain-specific capability profiles matter enormously for forecasting economic impact and dangerous capabilities, yet no systematic cross-domain comparison exists. Proposed Method: We operationalize the time horizon framework across six non-software domains by (1) curating 50-100 expert-timed tasks per domain with verified ground-truth evaluation rubrics, (2) recruiting domain experts (biologists, lawyers, financial analysts, etc.) to time themselves on representative tasks, (3) evaluating frontier models (GPT-5, Claude 4, Gemini 2.x) using domain-appropriate tool scaffolding, and (4) computing domain-specific 50% time horizons with confidence intervals. We additionally analyze whether cross-domain time horizons correlate, testing whether a single 'general capability' factor explains variance or whether domains exhibit independent scaling trajectories. Experiments: Human timing studies (N=30 experts per domain), AI evaluations across 300+ tasks, regression analysis of capability drivers per domain (tool use vs. reasoning vs. memory), and longitudinal comparison with software domain baselines from the anchor paper to quantify relative capability gaps and convergence rates.

title: Decomposing the Time Horizon Metric: Which Cognitive Substrates Drive AI Task Completion Scaling?
description: Problem: The anchor paper identifies that AI time horizons double every ~7 months, attributing gains to reliability, error recovery, logical reasoning, and tool use — but provides no quantitative decomposition of these factors. Without understanding which substrates drive scaling, we cannot predict capability trajectories, identify bottlenecks, or anticipate when dangerous capability thresholds will be crossed. Proposed Method: We construct a structured task battery of 200+ software tasks (30-180 min human completion time) where each task is annotated along four cognitive dimensions: error-recovery demand, multi-step logical chaining, tool orchestration complexity, and context-length dependency. We evaluate 8 frontier models (GPT-5, Claude 4, Gemini 2.x variants, open-source) on this battery, then fit a regression model predicting task success rate from model generation (as proxy for capability) interacted with cognitive dimension scores. We additionally design ablation tasks that surgically isolate each dimension (e.g., tasks with identical logic but varying error-recovery requirements). Experiments: (1) Measure relative contribution of each cognitive substrate to time-horizon improvements; (2) Test whether substrate contributions differ across model families (reasoning vs. non-reasoning); (3) Project which substrates are near saturation vs. still scaling rapidly; (4) Correlate substrate profiles with existing dangerous-capability evaluations to identify risk-relevant scaling signals.

title: Skill Decomposition of AI Time Horizons: Identifying Capability Bottlenecks Through Structured Task Taxonomy
description:
Problem: While the 50%-task-completion time horizon metric quantifies AI progress, it treats capability as a monolithic scalar. We lack understanding of *which specific sub-skills* are bottlenecking AI agents from extending their time horizons further, making it hard to predict non-linear capability jumps or design targeted improvements.

Proposed Method: We develop a hierarchical taxonomy decomposing long software tasks into atomic skill dimensions: (1) error recovery/adaptation, (2) multi-step planning, (3) tool orchestration, (4) context window management, (5) domain knowledge retrieval, and (6) specification ambiguity resolution. For each frontier model, we construct synthetic task variants that isolate individual skill dimensions by holding others constant, then measure per-dimension 50% time horizons separately. We fit a bottleneck model to predict overall task time horizon from individual skill horizons, identifying which skills impose binding constraints.

Experiments: Evaluate 6+ frontier models (GPT-5, Claude 3.7/4, Gemini 2.x series) on 200 tasks across the taxonomy spanning 5-minute to 8-hour human completion times. Compare predicted vs. observed overall time horizons. Measure skill-horizon correlation with wall-clock capability improvement over 2024-2026. Conduct ablation interventions (e.g., providing error hints) to validate bottleneck identification. Results will produce a skills-based capability roadmap and early-warning indicators for when specific skill breakthroughs might cause time-horizon jumps.

title: Beyond Time Horizons: Measuring AI Capability Degradation Under Resource Constraints and Interruption
description: Problem: The 50%-task-completion time horizon metric captures AI capability on uninterrupted, well-resourced tasks, but real-world software engineering involves context switching, resource limits (token budgets, API rate limits, memory constraints), and partial handoffs between human and AI. We lack metrics quantifying how AI capability degrades under these practical constraints. Proposed Method: We introduce 'constraint-adjusted time horizon' (CATH), which measures how the 50% success rate threshold shifts as a function of: (1) context window truncation mid-task, (2) forced interruptions requiring task resumption from checkpoints, (3) collaborative handoffs where humans complete partial work and AI resumes, and (4) compute/token budget caps. We construct a benchmark of 150 software tasks spanning 15-180 minute human completion times, systematically varying constraint severity. We measure both completion rate and solution quality degradation curves for frontier models (GPT-5, Claude 4, Gemini 2.x). Experiments: We compare degradation profiles across model families, task types (debugging vs. feature implementation vs. refactoring), and constraint types. We test whether checkpoint-based resumption strategies or explicit state-summarization prompting mitigates degradation. The key deliverable is a degradation taxonomy revealing which constraint types most severely limit real-world AI deployment, providing actionable guidance for human-AI workflow design.

title: Decomposing the Time Horizon Metric: Skill-Specific Capability Profiles for AI Software Agents
description: Problem: The 50%-task-completion time horizon provides a useful scalar summary of AI capability, but collapses heterogeneous skills (debugging, architecture design, API integration, testing, documentation) into a single number, obscuring where AI agents excel or fail relative to humans and hiding which capabilities are driving observed improvements. Method: We construct a fine-grained benchmark of ~400 software tasks explicitly tagged along six orthogonal skill dimensions—logical reasoning, tool use, error recovery, domain knowledge retrieval, multi-file coordination, and requirement disambiguation—with per-task human timing data collected from 80 professional developers stratified by experience level. For each dimension, we compute skill-specific time horizons and measure capability imbalance scores across five frontier models (GPT-5, Claude 4, Gemini 2.0 Ultra, Llama 4, Qwen 3). We then train a lightweight capability decomposition model that predicts composite time horizons from skill-specific sub-scores, validating on held-out task distributions. Experiments: (1) Rank dimensions by AI-vs-human capability gap; (2) measure whether skill imbalances predict failure modes on real GitHub issues; (3) test whether targeted fine-tuning on weak dimensions improves composite time horizon disproportionately; (4) analyze how skill profiles differ across model families. This produces actionable capability roadmaps for both benchmark designers and AI developers.

title: Beyond Time Horizons: Measuring AI Task Completion Under Realistic Collaboration and Interruption Conditions
description:
Problem: The 50%-task-completion time horizon metric assumes AI agents work in isolation on well-specified tasks, but real-world software engineering involves frequent human interruptions, clarification requests, partial handoffs, and collaborative workflows. Current benchmarks may overestimate practical autonomy by ignoring these friction points, or underestimate it by not allowing beneficial human-AI collaboration patterns.

Proposed Method: We introduce the 'collaborative time horizon' metric that extends the existing framework to measure AI effectiveness under three realistic conditions: (1) Interrupt-and-Resume tasks, where the AI must handle mid-task context switches and specification changes; (2) Human-in-the-Loop tasks, where humans can provide clarifying questions at defined checkpoints; (3) Partial-completion handoffs, where an AI picks up partially completed human work or vice versa. We instrument a modified scaffold to log collaboration patterns and develop a multi-dimensional capability profile beyond single scalar metrics.

Experiments: We recruit 30 professional software engineers to complete 100 tasks drawn from RE-Bench and new real-world GitHub issues under all three conditions with Claude 3.7, GPT-5, and Gemini 2.0. We measure completion rates, total wall-clock time including human intervention time, and error propagation rates. We compare against isolation-baseline metrics to quantify the 'collaboration gap' and identify which task categories benefit most from human partnership.

title: Decomposing the Time Horizon Metric: Skill Profiles and Bottleneck Analysis for Long-Horizon AI Tasks
description: Problem: The 50%-task-completion time horizon metric aggregates AI capability into a single scalar, obscuring *which* sub-skills drive progress or bottleneck performance. Understanding whether gains come from better planning, error recovery, tool use, or domain knowledge is critical for forecasting, safety monitoring, and targeted improvement. Proposed Method: We decompose long-horizon software tasks into a taxonomy of atomic skill dimensions (planning/decomposition, error detection/recovery, API/tool use, code synthesis, context tracking, logical reasoning) and annotate a dataset of ~500 tasks spanning RE-Bench, HCAST, and newly collected tasks with fine-grained skill labels and per-step observability logs from AI agents. We then train lightweight probes on agent execution traces to attribute success/failure to specific skill dimensions, producing per-model 'skill profiles.' We apply this to 6 frontier models (Claude 3.7, GPT-5, Gemini 2.0, etc.) and historical model versions. Experiments: (1) Validate skill taxonomy via inter-annotator agreement and ablation; (2) correlate skill profiles with overall time horizon scores; (3) measure how skill bottlenecks shift across model generations; (4) test whether skill profiles predict cross-domain generalization better than the aggregate metric. This provides a mechanistic decomposition of the time horizon trend and identifies which capabilities require the most attention for safe deployment.

title: Beyond Time Horizons: Measuring AI Robustness to Task Interruption and Handoff in Long-Horizon Software Engineering
description:
Problem: The 50%-task-completion time horizon metric captures AI capability on uninterrupted tasks, but real-world software engineering involves frequent context switches, partial handoffs between humans and AI, and resumption after interruptions. We lack understanding of how AI task completion degrades when tasks are interrupted mid-execution or when partial work must be transferred between agents or to humans.

Proposed Method: We introduce the 'Handoff Robustness Score' (HRS), measuring AI ability to (1) resume tasks from arbitrary mid-task checkpoints created by human developers, (2) complete tasks partially started by other AI agents, and (3) produce intermediate artifacts that humans can productively continue. We construct a benchmark of 150 software tasks (from RE-Bench and novel tasks) with human-annotated checkpoints at 25%, 50%, and 75% completion stages. We evaluate frontier models on cold-start resumption versus full task completion, measuring success rate degradation as a function of checkpoint position and artifact quality.

Experiments: We compare Claude 3.7 Sonnet, GPT-4o, and Gemini 2.0 on full-task versus checkpoint-resumption conditions; measure human productivity when continuing AI-generated partial work; and analyze whether time-horizon gains generalize to collaborative human-AI workflows. We expect significant degradation at mid-task handoffs, revealing a critical gap in current capability assessments with direct implications for AI-assisted software development pipelines.

title: Calibrating the Time Horizon Metric Across Cognitive Domains: Beyond Software Engineering
description:
Problem: The 50%-task-completion time horizon metric has been validated primarily for software engineering tasks, leaving unclear whether this metric generalizes to other cognitive domains (scientific reasoning, legal analysis, medical diagnosis, creative writing, mathematical research). Domain-specific task structures, error patterns, and human expertise distributions may cause the metric to behave differently, potentially inflating or deflating apparent AI capabilities when applied naively across contexts.

Proposed Method: We construct parallel benchmark suites across five cognitive domains (biomedical research, legal contract analysis, quantitative finance, academic mathematics, and structured creative writing), each spanning 2-minute to 8-hour human completion times. We recruit domain experts to time-annotate tasks under standardized conditions, then evaluate five frontier AI models (including Claude 3.7 Sonnet, GPT-5, and Gemini 2.0) on each suite. We compute per-domain time horizons, analyze calibration across domains, and identify structural task features (e.g., iterative feedback loops, external tool dependency, ambiguity tolerance) that predict where AI time horizons diverge from software benchmarks.

Experiments: (1) Cross-domain time horizon comparison with 95% confidence intervals, (2) regression analysis linking task structural features to AI-human performance gaps, (3) longitudinal comparison using archived model evaluations to test whether doubling rates differ by domain, (4) ablation study on how expert pool diversity affects human baseline timing estimates.

title: Task Decomposition Depth as a Predictor of AI Completion Rate: Mapping the Hierarchical Complexity Frontier
description: Problem: The 50%-task-completion time horizon metric aggregates over diverse task structures, obscuring *why* AI fails on longer tasks. Tasks taking equivalent human time may differ dramatically in hierarchical decomposition depth (number of nested subtask dependencies), which may better predict AI failure than raw duration alone. Method: We instrument a large set of software tasks (extending RE-Bench and HCAST) with explicit dependency graphs, measuring decomposition depth, branching factor, and inter-subtask coupling. We train a failure-prediction model using these structural features alongside task duration, then test whether decomposition depth explains variance in AI success rates beyond what time horizon alone predicts. We also investigate whether AI models implicitly construct correct decomposition plans (via chain-of-thought analysis) and whether decomposition quality mediates task success. Experiments: (1) Annotate 200+ tasks with dependency graphs using expert annotators; (2) run Claude 3.7 Sonnet, GPT-5, and Gemini 2.0 on this suite logging intermediate states; (3) correlate structural graph metrics with success rates controlling for task duration; (4) ablation: provide explicit decomposition hints to measure impact on time horizon. Expected outcome: Decomposition depth is a stronger predictor than time alone, suggesting that improving hierarchical planning is the key bottleneck to extending AI time horizons.

title: Decomposing the Time Horizon Metric: Which Cognitive Sub-Skills Drive AI Task Completion Scaling?
description: Problem: The 50%-task-completion time horizon metric reveals that frontier AI capability is growing rapidly, but attributes this to broad factors like 'reliability,' 'logical reasoning,' and 'tool use.' We then train interpretable regression models predicting per-task AI success rates from sub-skill demand profiles, using performance data from 6+ frontier models. Experiments: (1) Identify which sub-skills most predict failure at each time-horizon tier; (2) Track how sub-skill bottlenecks shift across model generations (GPT-4 through 2025 frontier models); (3) Validate by constructing targeted synthetic tasks that isolate individual sub-skills and measuring whether predicted bottlenecks generalize. This yields a mechanistic decomposition of the time horizon scaling trend, enabling more precise capability forecasting and identification of safety-relevant capability thresholds.

title: Decomposing the Time Horizon Metric: Measuring AI Reliability, Error Recovery, and Reasoning as Independent Capability Dimensions
description: Problem: The 50%-task-completion time horizon metric conflates multiple distinct capabilities (reliability, error recovery, logical reasoning, tool use) into a single scalar. This makes it difficult to diagnose bottlenecks, predict capability jumps, or design targeted improvements. Understanding which sub-capabilities drive time horizon growth is essential for both capability forecasting and safety analysis. Proposed Method: We develop a fine-grained capability decomposition framework that independently measures four sub-dimensions identified in the anchor paper: (1) step-level reliability (error rate per atomic action), (2) error detection latency (how quickly the model recognizes mistakes), (3) recovery success rate (ability to course-correct after identified errors), and (4) multi-step logical planning depth. We instrument existing long-horizon task benchmarks (RE-Bench, HCAST, SWE-bench Verified) with execution traces that log intermediate states, enabling post-hoc attribution of task failures to specific sub-dimensions. We then fit a multiplicative capability model predicting overall time horizon from these four factors. Experiments: We evaluate 8 frontier models (GPT-4o, Claude 3.7, Gemini 2.0, DeepSeek-R2, etc.), measure each sub-dimension independently, validate the decomposition model's predictive accuracy on held-out tasks, and analyze how each sub-dimension has evolved over model generations. This enables more precise extrapolation and identifies which capabilities require targeted development or monitoring for safety purposes.

title: Decomposing the Time Horizon Metric: Isolating Capability Bottlenecks That Limit AI Task Completion Duration
description: Problem: The 50%-task-completion time horizon metric captures aggregate AI capability growth but obscures *which* specific sub-capabilities drive performance on longer tasks. Understanding whether planning, error recovery, tool use, context management, or domain reasoning is the binding constraint would enable targeted improvements and more precise capability forecasting. Proposed Method: We decompose long software tasks into a taxonomy of atomic capability requirements (multi-step planning, error detection/recovery, API/tool orchestration, long-context retention, domain knowledge application). We construct a controlled benchmark of ~200 tasks where each task isolates one or two capability dimensions while holding others constant, with matched human timing data. For each frontier model, we fit a capability bottleneck model that predicts task success probability as a function of capability scores, identifying which dimensions most sharply limit performance as task duration increases. We additionally propose a 'capability ceiling test': artificially providing oracle assistance on individual dimensions (e.g., perfect error detection) and measuring the resulting time horizon boost. Experiments: Evaluate GPT-4o, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, Gemini 2.0 Pro on the decomposed benchmark; measure time horizon per capability dimension; validate bottleneck predictions against held-out naturalistic tasks from RE-Bench; compare bottleneck profiles across model families to identify architectural vs. training-driven capability gaps.
